lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the price of being early
lead.head: Right too early, damned for it
body: It is a cold winter afternoon in early nineteenth-century London. A girl sits by her mother’s grave behind St Pancras Church and traces the letters on the stone with a finger. That, Amit Varma said, is how she learned to write. {061-S01}

Varma, who had written the scene himself, read it out as a quiz for Ajay Shah. Shah guessed Mary Wollstonecraft. She was the mother. The girl was Mary Shelley, and both women, Varma said, wrote books that changed the world.
The mother had died of an infection a few days after giving birth. The daughter would forever feel guilt that her birth had killed her mother.
Progress happens really slowly, Varma said. In every age some people think things that later seem completely normal but are radical at the time.
“And often they are shunned and despised and treated in horrible ways,” he said. The hosts called them the outlaws.
## A relay race of dates

Varma’s first three outlaws, he said, could be one interlocking web series. Wollstonecraft read John Locke on equal rights for all men and asked where women stood. Horace Walpole called her a “hyena in petticoats”.
Mary Shelley wrote *Frankenstein* at eighteen, before science fiction existed as a genre. The typical reaction was that her husband must have written it.

Ignaz Semmelweis, born in 1818, the year of *Frankenstein*, cut deaths in a Vienna maternity ward by making doctors wash their hands. He could not explain why it worked, and he died in a lunatic asylum.

The threads tie together. Wollstonecraft’s fatal infection, Varma said, came from a doctor who had not washed his hands. Told in parallel, “it begins and ends with hand washing, it begins and ends with childbirth, it begins and ends in death”.
## Where is the mechanism?
Shah answered with outlaws of science: Alfred Wegener, who saw that the continents had drifted apart; Boltzmann, whose physics rested on atoms nobody had seen; the monk Mendel; and Darwin.

Their common trouble, Shah said, was a missing explanation. Each had evidence and good predictions but no account of how. “Last mile problem. Darwin did not have the explanation. So this is a recurrent theme we’ll see again and again.” {061-C07}
Varma reached for the Planck principle, that science changes one funeral at a time, and warned of survivor bias: we remember only the outlaws who were eventually vindicated.
## Why so hostile?

What puzzled Varma was the hostility. Drawing on an essay by Paul Graham, he said being conventional-minded is understandable, but the aggressively conventional-minded are the greatest danger. {061-C10}

Shah’s answer was the establishment of institutions, credentials, journals, jobs and funding. A disruptive idea threatens people’s own lives. “It’s the same as any other bureaucracy,” he said. “What bureaucracies want is to keep the boat going.” {061-C12}
He also offered a selfish remedy. Since most people ignore mavericks, listening to them is an arbitrage opportunity. “This is a $500 bill lying on the ground,” he said. {061-C13}
Better, he said, to spend an hour with a mad person than with a sane one. “That’s why I do the show with you,” Varma replied.
Shah ended with a place rather than a book: Boltzmann’s tombstone in Vienna, which bears the equation S = k ln W.

second.label: The vaccine pioneer
second.head: Grant, grant, no, no, no
second.deck: Amit Varma on Katalin Karikó, rejected for years before mRNA vaccines
body: Katalin Karikó’s early research on mRNA was treated as a joke, Amit Varma said, something on the fringes. She applied for grant after grant, and every time the answer was no. {061-S13}

She applied for a faculty position at the University of Pennsylvania and was told she was not of faculty quality. It took years, Varma said, until “the moment met the woman”. mRNA vaccines proved a miracle, and in a sense, he said, she saved the planet.

Varma then turned the story around. We remember such people because they were eventually vindicated, even after death. For each of them, others were right and never redeemed. He guessed that only one in a million make it. {061-C09}

quote.text: every night I was working grant, grant, grant, and every time the reply came back, no, no, no.

third.head: Small print run, big idea
body: Mendel was an obscure monk in Austria, Ajay Shah said, who tried to turn what every plant and animal breeder knew by instinct into laws of inheritance. He was lucky to choose a simple plant, the pea.

It was one of the most important moments in the history of science, and he published it quietly. Printing was expensive: the print run for his paper was 40, all he could afford, and he sent copies to a few people. {061-S10}
Those who read it shrugged, Shah said. Plant breeding was nothing new to them, and they missed the magnificence of what Mendel had found.
“If biology has to be more than stamp collecting,” Shah said, “then it is the child of Mendel and Darwin.” {061-J10}

p2.title: Ahead of their time
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why radical ideas, and the people who hold them, are shunned. {061-C01}

sections.label: The mother
sections.head: Taking Locke at his word
sections.caption: Wollstonecraft and the rights of woman
body: Mary Wollstonecraft was born in 1759, Amit Varma said, into times that were not good for women. {#born} Wives could not own property or initiate divorce, and it was legal for a husband to beat his wife.
She was one of seven children of an alcoholic, violent father. Her rescue came from a neighbour, Reverend Henry Clare, who introduced her to the works of John Locke.
Locke, Varma’s intellectual hero, held that we are all born with the right to self-ownership, from which every other right flows: to free speech, to property, to life. {061-C02}
## What about women?
Locke also inspired the American Declaration of Independence. Wollstonecraft, Varma said, read its line that all men are born equal and demanded to know what was meant by all men. {061-S02}

Her *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, in 1792, argued that a false education made women slaves of the male gaze, and that virtue should flow from reason, not religion, tradition or convention. That, Varma said, challenged every construct of society. {061-C03}
The book was received very badly. Thomas Taylor replied with *A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes*: if women can have rights, why not animals?

~ Varma found one thing tragic. Writing for men who read political philosophy, she had to argue that freed women would be better daughters, wives and mothers, not that they would live autonomous, fulfilling lives.

quote.text: Our species is special because we are capable of reason.

sections.label: The daughter
sections.head: Science fiction from scratch
sections.caption: Frankenstein, written at eighteen
body: Mary Shelley grew up among books, in her father William Godwin’s salon, and ran away with Percy Shelley, who was already married.

Around 1816, Amit Varma said, she sat by a fire with Percy Shelley, Lord Byron and John Polidori. Polidori described the anatomist William Lawrence’s lectures arguing that there was no soul, only the organs of the body. Percy Shelley wondered whether humans had created God.
Add John Milton’s *Paradise Lost*, one of her early influences, and “you see *Frankenstein* coming to birth”, Varma said.
She was eighteen. Science fiction did not exist, and she had no models of the craft. Yet she told her story in three voices, nested one inside another: a ship’s captain, Frankenstein and his monster.
## Where clichés began
Readers today may find it clumsy and full of clichés. “Do not judge her for those clichés because they started there,” Varma said. “They weren’t clichés there.” {061-C05}

Its question, whether a being we create has rights, is live again with artificial intelligence. “I think the biggest questions of modern times are actually tackled by science fiction,” he said. {061-C06}
~ The book was ignored, and many assumed her husband had written it. Percy Shelley may have written about 4,000 of its 78,000 words, Varma said, and they stand out as bad writing. {#fourthousand}

quote.text: Here is someone writing without a model for a genre that does not exist, and just coming up with a miraculous book.

sections.label: The doctor
sections.head: Clean hands, dirty politics
sections.caption: Semmelweis and the two maternity wards
body: Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian physician, was born in 1818, the year of *Frankenstein*. In 1846 he joined Vienna General Hospital as an assistant to the obstetrician, Amit Varma said.
One maternity ward had a mortality rate of 10 per cent, the other 4 per cent. {#wards} Women begged to be put in the second.

Overcrowding was not the cause: the safer ward was more crowded. Nor was the weather, since the wards were close together. The clue came when a colleague died after being poked by a scalpel, with the symptoms of childbed fever. Staff in Ward One also worked on corpses.
## Wash, and live
Semmelweis made them wash their hands in a chlorinated solution. Deaths fell from 18 per cent in one recorded month to two, then one, and to zero within two years. {#eighteen}
But there was no germ theory yet. “He solved the problem without knowing why,” Varma said. {061-S05} Doctors, a higher social class, were offended at being called unclean.
One German physician who believed him realised a loved one had died because he attended her with unwashed hands, and killed himself. {061-S06}
~ Semmelweis was sacked over departmental politics. In 1865 he died in a lunatic asylum, of a gangrenous arm, two weeks after guards beat him and locked him in a dark cell.

quote.text: Am I being blamed for all the deaths that came before?
quote.who: Ajay Shah, voicing the offended doctors

sections.label: The pattern
sections.head: Show me the mechanism
sections.caption: the missing mechanism
body: Why are true ideas rejected? The recurring reason, Ajay Shah said, is that they work before anyone can explain how. {061-C07}

Semmelweis had no germ theory. Alfred Wegener could not say what force moved continents. Boltzmann could not show anyone an atom. Darwin’s critics demanded to see where the code of the finch was written.

Even a proven fix can wait. Shah recalled the childhood story of scurvy, solved by carrying preserved lime, because sailors lacked only vitamin C. “When you go examine the dates carefully, it’s like decades went by,” he said. {061-S07}
## One funeral at a time
Amit Varma cited the Planck principle. Playing the long game, he said, is cold comfort when, as Keynes put it, in the long run we are all dead. {061-C08}

He had just been in Washington, DC, where his friend Vikram Raghavan pointed out a building in which Keynes had a heart attack under a staircase. “So did he say in the short run we are all dead?” Varma asked. Keynes survived. {061-J05}
~ Shah compared Darwin’s delay with Newton, who sat on the calculus while Leibniz rushed to publish. “It’s like I’m Newton,” he said. “Once I understand it, how can humans understand it?” {061-J04}

quote.text: It reminds me of the Planck principle, science changes one funeral at a time.

sections.label: The conformists
sections.head: Why the herd bites
sections.caption: the aggressively conventional-minded
body: Amit Varma took his frame from Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism*: people are conventional-minded or independent-minded, and passive or aggressive. Wallace, Varma said, was aggressively independent-minded, Darwin passively so. {061-C10}
Being conventional-minded he could understand, as cognitive laziness or even rationality. What flummoxed him was the aggression.

He had met it himself. When he wrote a column arguing that population is a good thing, readers reflexively attacked him instead of the argument. School had taught them population was the problem, and they had tied the belief to themselves. {061-S14}
## Ridicule at scale

Social media makes it worse, he said. Echoing Adam Mastroianni, he argued that Wegener’s fellow professionals may have treated him with disdain. “Today the whole world will. And that is such a disincentive.” {061-C11}
Ajay Shah’s answer was that people are tacitly upholding a system of institutions, credentials, journals, jobs and funding, and protecting their own lives. {061-C12}
Every rung of an academic career, from school exams to tenure, rewards keeping your head down, he said. Of five personality traits, only conscientiousness is selected for. {061-C15}
~ His remedy was self-interest. We should change our filters, which demand a clean shirt, the right jokes and being one of the gang.

quote.text: The very act of imagination, the very act of creativity is probably grounded in being a bit of a weirdo

contQuote.text: Everyone will say Darwin, wow, Mendel, wow. But there are Darwins and Mendels around us who we probably ignore and we think of them as weird and we’re not taking them seriously.

stories.start: in the field of geology, there is in a way, one of the great
stories.end: and India smashed into uh Eurasia and made the Himalayas
stories.caption: Alfred Wegener and the moving continents
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the geologist who read a map too well
stories.head: Continents move, minds don’t
body: Alfred Wegener got his idea by staring at a map, Ajay Shah said. The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa seemed to fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. {061-S08}
“Just imagine how many people would have looked at that same map,” Shah said.

Wegener turned the hunch into testable claims. If the continents had once been joined, the fossil record should show the same creatures on both sides. It did. The rock formations should match. They did. He found similar correspondences elsewhere.
He began to dream, Shah said, that about 260 million years ago all the land was one supercontinent, known as Pangaea, which split apart and drifted. {#pangaea}
His contemporaries asked for the mechanism: what mighty force could be yanking continents apart? When he wrote his first book in 1912, it was greeted with derision. {#derision}

Amit Varma found that especially tragic. Wegener was no outsider but “a freaking geologist”, thinking rationally, with fossils and rock formations adding up, respected until he went beyond convention.

He kept struggling against the establishment, keen to prove his hypotheses in Greenland, and died there on an expedition in 1930. {#greenland} Only in the 1960s did the idea win wide acceptance, recast as plate tectonics.
~ Shah remembers it as hot new science in his father’s day: India splitting off near Madagascar and smashing into Eurasia to push up the Himalayas.
stories.why: The evidence lay on a map anyone could read. It took one person to look, and decades for the field to catch up, because nobody could yet say what moved the continents.

stories.start: I want to turn to Charles Darwin. I guess all of us know
stories.end: And suddenly we have the first theory of biology, this is like Newtonian physics.
stories.caption: Darwin, Wallace and evolution
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on one theory, cracked twice
stories.head: Twenty-two years and a fever
body: Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle, gathering specimens. By 1837, thinking about the finches and iguanas of the Galapagos, Ajay Shah said, he had grasped the theory of evolution.
He also saw at once that it was a personal disaster. {061-S11} Tell the world that God did not create us, and they would cut off his head. So he polished his book, year after year.

Darwin, Shah told Amit Varma, “was as great a book writer as you”. {061-J01} Meanwhile Alfred Russel Wallace, delirious with malaria in the jungles of Indonesia, cracked the same theory from scratch. {#malaria}
~ Wallace, with a bias for action, came home ready to present. Friends at the Royal Society who knew of Darwin’s secret project arranged a joint presentation in 1859.

quote.text: And as he understood it, he also understood this is a personal disaster.

stories.postscript: Varma, on Darwin’s 22 years: “I have time, I have time.” {#time}

stories.start: Another uh story of a similar nature is uh the great physicist Boltzmann
stories.end: He just missed it by a few years.
stories.caption: Boltzmann’s unseen atoms
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a physicist who missed his moment
stories.head: Nobody had seen an atom
body: In the 1860s and 1870s, Ajay Shah said, the physicist Boltzmann helped make the leap from the kinetic theory of gases, where molecules are hard dots obeying deterministic rules, to statistical mechanics, which uses probability through and through.
It explained temperature and entropy and gave good predictions. But no microscope of the late nineteenth century could see an atom, and sceptics asked whether anyone had ever seen one.

Boltzmann had a terrible time. He did not get jobs, was thrown out of his home university in Vienna, and killed himself in 1906. “And it just is so unlucky that this was a couple of years before all his stuff worked out,” Shah said. {061-S09}
~ The stories, Shah said, all come from Jacob Bronowski’s book and BBC series *The Ascent of Man*. {061-R13}
stories.why: Being a free thinker, Shah said, is a lonely and challenging quest against jobs, careers and an establishment. Conformity is the easy path. Vindication can arrive just after you are gone.

stories.start: there were enough stories to tell of Jon Snow and W C Panell
stories.end: told in a wonderful book by Jinme Tumbe called Age of Pandemics
stories.caption: the cholera map and caste
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a disease map that exposed caste
stories.head: Barred from the well, spared
body: In mid-nineteenth-century London, Amit Varma said, John Snow worked out that cholera is caused by water. The finding met tremendous resistance, and it took decades, especially in India, to be accepted.
Near the end of the century, another investigator made a cholera map of an Indian village. It showed that most of those who died were of a higher caste. {061-S12}
The reason was a well of contaminated water, which the lower castes were not allowed to use. “The only person from a lower caste who got cholera was a washerman who washed their clothes,” Varma said.
~ These links, he said, were just not accepted. He credited the story to Chinmay Tumbe’s “wonderful book”, *Age of Pandemics*. {061-R12}
stories.why: Data can expose a society’s structure as sharply as a disease’s route. Here exclusion, ironically, protected the excluded, and even so plain a link took decades to win acceptance in India.

quiz.q: In the scene Amit Varma read out, how did the young Mary Shelley learn to write?
quiz.a: By tracing the letters on her mother’s gravestone in St Pancras churchyard.

quiz.q: To which thinker’s works did the neighbour Reverend Henry Clare introduce the young Mary Wollstonecraft?
quiz.a: John Locke, whose philosophy grounds every other right in self-ownership.

quiz.q: What did Ignaz Semmelweis make staff do after handling corpses and before examining mothers?
quiz.a: Wash their hands in a chlorinated solution he had prepared himself.

quiz.q: Why was the print run of Mendel’s paper on inheritance in peas only 40?
quiz.a: Printing was expensive, and 40 copies were all he could afford.

quiz.q: Where was Alfred Russel Wallace when he cracked the theory of evolution from scratch?
quiz.a: In the jungles of Indonesia, delirious with a malarial fever.

quiz.q: In Paul Graham’s four quadrants, which group poses the greatest danger to new ideas?
quiz.a: The aggressively conventional-minded, who react with hostility to ideas that challenge them.
